issues.issue: The execution date is rendered as an illegible fragment ("/ Oo} 24) OO , 2000"), leaving the date of the instrument uncertain on its face. That is a mechanical defect in the operative creation language.

The recital commits to "less than 100 Shareholders" while operative Section 4.4 caps the Trust at "not more than 100 Shareholders", a one-shareholder divergence between recital and operative text. A court asked about the shareholder ceiling would have to reconcile the two.

The definition directs the reader to "Article Nine, Section 9.2" for the meaning of "Covered Person", but Section 9.2 (Trustee Action; Expert Advice) contains no such definition. The mis-citation is a mechanical error in the defined term itself.

"Covered Person" is in fact defined in Article Eight, Section 8.1, so the definitional cross-reference cannot be squared with the body of the instrument. The reach of every exculpation and indemnity clause turns on which text supplies the definition.

"Majority Shareholder Vote" is defined but never used in any operative provision, and Section 4.8 denies Shareholders any voting rights at all. The definition cannot be reconciled with Section 4.8's blanket denial of the franchise.

Section 5.2 states that upon redemption "Shares shall not be canceled and may be reissued", while this definition excludes repurchased or redeemed Shares held in treasury from Outstanding Shares. The overlap matters for the two-thirds Outstanding Shares removal vote in Section 2.2(b).

Shares are defined as "transferable units of interest", but Section 4.9 declares the beneficial interest of a Shareholder non-transferable and any purported transfer void. The definition and Section 4.9 point in opposite directions on transferability.
The definition is circular — "'Trust' means the Trust, created hereby" — defining the term by itself. The circularity is a drafting defect, though the referent is obvious from the opening paragraph.

The definition contemplates plural "Trustees acting collectively" while Section 2.2(a) provides that "[t]here shall be one trustee". The plural-Trustee machinery in Sections 2.3 and 2.4 rests on this unresolved gap.

The declaration that any good-faith determination of the Trust's interests "shall be conclusive" sits against Section 3.3, which subjects the Trustee to a prudent-person ERISA fiduciary standard, and Section 8.5, which preserves ERISA Part 4 liability. Whether conclusiveness survives those provisions is a real question.

"There shall be one trustee, except as the Trustee may determine otherwise" leaves the number of trustees wholly at large, with no stated maximum or mechanism. The exception swallows the rule it qualifies.

Sections 2.3 and 2.4 repeatedly speak of "the remaining Trustees" and "a majority of the Trustees", machinery that presupposes a plural board this section says does not exist. The two cannot be read together without straining.

This clause lets Shareholders remove the Trustee by a two-thirds vote of Outstanding Shares at a meeting, while Section 4.8 states Shareholders have "no right ... to appoint, select, vote for or remove the Trustee". That is a direct contradiction between two operative provisions.

Vacancy-filling is committed to "the remaining Trustee or Trustees", which fails when Section 2.2(a)'s single Trustee resigns or is removed, leaving no one to appoint a successor. Section 2.2(b) also contemplates a successor being "elected", which no provision provides for given Section 4.8.

The section vests all powers in "the remaining Trustees" during a vacancy, which cannot operate under Section 2.2(a)'s single-trustee structure where a vacancy leaves none remaining. The delegation-by-power-of-attorney sentence likewise assumes other Trustees exist.

The final sentence is garbled and its cross-reference incomplete ("as provided In ... 1.2 proportionate undivided-beneficial interest ... Article Four"), so the nature of a Shareholder's beneficial interest is stated unintelligibly. The reader cannot tell which Article Four provision governs.

The Trustee may make "any investments which it, in its sole discretion, deems proper", yet must remain "consistent with the investment objectives established by the Trustee" — a self-referential limit whose content the Trustee itself sets. Whether the limit is a real constraint or none at all is genuinely contestable.

The disclaimer that the Trustee is not "bound by current or future laws or customs applicable to trust investments" cannot be squared with Section 3.3, which imposes the ERISA prudent-person standard, or with Section 8.5's preservation of ERISA Part 4 duties. A court would have to decide which governs the Trustee's investment conduct.

This section authorises the Trustee to buy from, sell to and lend Trust assets to itself and its affiliates, while the closing paragraph of Section 3.1 requires the Trust to comply with the affiliated-transaction prohibitions of Section 17(a), (d) and (e) of the 1940 Act as if registered. The permission and the prohibition cover the same ground.

The prudent-person standard imposed here runs against Article Eight's exculpation provisions (Sections 8.1 and 8.4), which limit Covered Person liability to bad faith, gross negligence or wilful misconduct and substitute contractual duties for those at law. Section 8.5 only partially reconciles them, and only for ERISA plans.

The passage stating each Share's entitlement is corrupt and unreadable ("except-te affected. hy expense allocatign non-redemntion hares"), so the exception to pro rata treatment cannot be determined. The scope of the "expense allocations" carve-out is unascertainable from the text.

The opening sentences are mutilated ("The number of Shares Q eries is unl ... each Share shail have a par value (if 2"), leaving the share-number limit and par value unstated. The operative terms of the Shares are missing on the face of the section.

Eligibility requirements are merely permissive ("may, in its sole discretion, establish"), whereas Recital (b) states the Trust relies on the Section 3(c)(7) qualified-purchaser exemption and Section 4.4 imposes a hard shareholder cap. A discretionary admission power sits awkwardly with mandatory eligibility limits.

The operative limit is corrupted in the text ("the—Trust-shali-- ~hot_heve_morethan_100- Shareholders at any me curma KS sxistence"), and "a principal purpose" in the look-through test is undefined. The look-through condition (ii) makes the cap turn on subjective purpose.

Recital (c) commits to "less than 100 Shareholders" while this section permits "not more than 100", so recital and operative provision state different ceilings. The mismatch matters to the publicly-traded-partnership objective both recite.

The concluding sentences on charging general liabilities are badly corrupted ("teserves of the Trust which ar as_ belonging to .an particular Series shall be allocated and charged"), so the rule for allocating unattributable liabilities is unreadable. "Fair and equitable" allocation is in any event left wholly to the Trustee's conclusive judgment.

The absolute inter-series liability shield is qualified by "unless otherwise provided in this Declaration" and is subject to the Trustee's allocation power in Section 4.6(a) and its lien over Series assets under Article Seven. Whether those provisions cut into the shield is arguable.
The register is to record "all Share transfers", yet Section 4.9 makes Shares non-transferable and any purported transfer void. The recording obligation presupposes transfers the Declaration forbids.

The section empowers the Trustee to "make rules governing the transfer of Shares", while Section 4.9 declares the beneficial interest non-transferable and any transfer void. The two provisions assume opposite answers on whether transfers can occur.

The blanket denial of any right to "vote for or remove the Trustee" contradicts Section 2.2(b)(ii), which permits removal of the Trustee by a two-thirds vote of Outstanding Shares at a Shareholder meeting. The denial of any right to amend also sits against the proviso in Section 9.7 (Amendments) allowing Shareholders to vote on submitted amendments.

Non-transferability contradicts the Article One definition of "Shares" as "transferable units of interest" and Section 4.7's register of "all Share transfers" and rules "governing the transfer of Shares". A court would have to decide whether any transfer mechanism survives.

Distributions must be "pro rata ... in proportion to the number of Shares", while Section 4.1 qualifies each holder's pro rata entitlement "except to the extent affected by expense allocations" and Section 9.3(a) allows Series payments to be reduced by allocated charges. The unqualified pro rata rule here does not carry those carve-outs.

The in-kind redemption sentence is fragmentary and unreadable ("may be wholly OL paruy Value of such securities or assets used, in such determination of Net Asset Value"), so the conditions for paying redemptions in securities rather than cash cannot be ascertained. Whether a Shareholder can be forced to take assets in kind, and at what valuation, is left open.

Section 5.2's opening grants each Shareholder the right to redeem "at a redemption price per Share equal to their Net Asset Value next determined", which assumes a cash price, while this sentence permits payment wholly or partly in securities. Section 5.3's NAV machinery does not say how in-kind assets are to be valued for this purpose.

NAV is to be determined "in a manner consistent with the 1940 Act" even though Recital (b) states the Trust is intended to be exempt from 1940 Act registration under Section 3(c)(7). Which 1940 Act requirements are imported for valuation purposes is left unstated.

Section 5.2 permits the Trustee to suspend redemptions only "for a period not exceeding seven days", whereas this section says Shareholders "shall have no right of redemption or payment until the Trustee declares the end of the suspension", with no outside limit. It also refers to the Trustee "postpon[ing] payment of the redemption price", a power Section 5.2 does not expressly confer.

The bar on retaining the Trustee or affiliates for "additional services for additional compensation beyond that disclosed and agreed to" in the separate securities lending agreements ties this Declaration to outside documents, while Sections 2.6 and 3.1(k) let the Trustee fix its own compensation. Which instrument controls Trustee compensation is not resolved.

The safe harbour for affiliated contracts is conditioned on the contract being "reasonable and fair", a standard the section neither defines nor assigns anyone to determine. The proviso's content is left entirely at large.

Validating contracts with affiliates conflicts with the closing paragraph of Section 3.1, which requires compliance with the 1940 Act Section 17(a), (d) and (e) prohibitions on affiliated transactions as if the Trust were registered. The two provisions treat affiliate dealing differently.

The expense list is a long enumeration closed by open-ended catch-alls — "including, but not limited to", "such non-recurring items as may arise" and "all losses and liabilities incurred by it in administering the Trust" — so the reach of the catch-all against the specifics is uncertain. Whether litigation losses caused by the Trustee's own conduct fall within it is exactly the kind of ejusdem generis question this framing invites.

The Article is expressed to be "Subject to Article Four, Section 4.4", but Section 4.4 concerns the 100-Shareholder publicly-traded-partnership cap and has nothing to do with expenses; the series-expense rules are in Section 4.6. The cross-reference cannot be made to work with the rest of the instrument.

Liability is preserved only for "bad faith, gross negligence, wilful misconduct or reckless disregard of the duties involved", terms the Declaration nowhere defines, and the carve-out is partly corrupted in the text. Where ordinary negligence ends and "gross negligence" begins is the classic contestable line.

The exculpation cannot be squared with Section 3.3, which makes the Trustee an ERISA fiduciary held to the prudent-person standard, or with Section 8.5, which says Article Eight shall not relieve the Trustee of ERISA Part 4 duties. A court would have to fix which standard governs a Shareholder's claim.

Subparagraph (ii) is ungrammatical as a completion of the lead-in — the Trust "shall indemnify ... including ... (ii) apply to all claims" — so it is unclear whether (ii) states an indemnity or merely a definitional gloss. The mismatch changes what the mandatory indemnity actually covers.

Indemnity is mandatory for anything incurred "by virtue of ... having been a Covered Person" with no conduct exclusion, whereas Section 8.1 preserves liability for bad faith, gross negligence and wilful misconduct. Read literally the Trust must indemnify conduct Section 8.1 says is not excused.

The subsection speaks of "[a]ny repeal or modification of this Article Seven" although it sits in Article Eight, and Article Seven is the expenses article. The mis-numbering leaves it uncertain which Article the anti-retroactivity protection attaches to.

Immunity for "good faith reliance on the provisions of this Declaration" sits against Section 3.3's ERISA prudent-person duty and Section 8.5, which says Article Eight shall not relieve the Trustee of any ERISA Part 4 fiduciary obligation. Whether reliance on the Declaration can defeat a statutory fiduciary claim is left unresolved.

The sentence purports to "replace" all duties and liabilities "otherwise existing at law or in equity" without identifying which provisions do the restricting or which duties are displaced. The scope of the substitution is left entirely to inference.

A wholesale replacement of duties existing at law or in equity cannot be reconciled with Section 3.3's express acknowledgment of ERISA fiduciary status or with Section 8.5, which preserves ERISA Part 4 responsibilities notwithstanding Article Eight. The provisions pull in opposite directions on the Trustee's residual duties.

The carve-out saves only liabilities imposed "by Part 4 of ERISA", leaving unclear how much of Sections 8.1 and 8.4 survives as to ERISA plan Shareholders whose Trustee is held to the prudent-person standard in Section 3.3. The boundary between the exculpation and the exception is where any dispute would sit.

This section states "[t]his Declaration creates a trust and not a partnership", while the First Amendment deletes it and substitutes a Section 9.1 requiring each Series to be classified and taxed as a partnership under Subchapter K. Anyone reading the instrument as a whole must decide which text governs and for what purposes.

The section is "[s]ubject to the provisions of Article Eight" in one sentence and "subject to the provisions of Article Seven" two sentences later for the same exculpation subject-matter, though Article Seven is the expenses article. One of the two cross-references must be wrong.
Article One's definition of "Covered Person" points to "Article Nine, Section 9.2", but this section contains no such definition. The definitional chain breaks here.

The Trust is given "perpetual existence" and then, in the same subsection, the Trustee may sell all assets and "dissolve the Trust" without Shareholder approval. The sale clause also permits conveyance only "to another Series" while the consideration clause speaks of "such Series, entity, or series thereof", leaving the permitted transferee uncertain.

The second paragraph refers to a merger "approved by the Trustees in accordance with this Section 4", but the section is Section 9.4 and there is no Section 4. The mis-citation obscures which approval the merger agreement must satisfy.

A merger agreement is said to be able to "effect any amendment to the Declaration or effect the adoption of a new governing Declaration" without Shareholder action, which stands against the proviso in Section 9.7 (Amendments) giving Shareholders a right to vote on amendments submitted to them. The two amendment routes are not harmonised.

The choice of Maryland law is subject to an exception where "it may otherwise be pre-empted by ERISA", leaving the boundary between Maryland trust law and ERISA to be worked out against Sections 3.3 and 8.5. Which body of law supplies the Trustee's duties is not settled by this provision.

The section says the Declaration "may be amended without Shareholder approval" and then, by proviso, that "Shareholders shall have the right to vote on any amendment submitted to them by the Trustee in its discretion" — a proviso that both grants a vote and leaves it wholly optional. The premise that the Declaration "does not confer any independent rights to Shareholders" is also contradicted by the rights it elsewhere grants.

Section 4.8 states Shareholders "shall have no right to amend ... this Declaration of Trust", which cannot be squared with this section's proviso conferring a right to vote on amendments. The section is also numbered 9.7, the same number as the following Fiscal Year section.

This section is numbered "9.7", the same number already used by the preceding Amendments section, so a reference to Section 9.7 elsewhere is indeterminate. It also says the fiscal year end is "determined by the Trustee in this Declaration" although the Declaration fixes no date.

Severance is triggered by the Trustee's own determination, with counsel, that a provision conflicts with the Maryland Act, the 1940 Act or other law, and the provision is then "deemed never to have constituted a part of this Declaration". Whether that unilateral power can operate on provisions protecting Shareholders, such as Sections 3.3 and 8.5, is open.

The execution date is left as an unfilled fragment ("as of the ap day of November, 2001"), so the effective date of the amendment is not ascertainable from the instrument. The closing clause compounds this by making it effective "as of the date first above written".

The operative allocation language is corrupted and incomplete ("shall allocate (i) all income — i j ors percentage Interest in the serie e d and loss based on the full netting methodology"), so the required allocation rules cannot be read. It also invokes "the IRC" and "§1.704-3(e)(3)(v)" without the defined term "Code" used throughout Article One.

Treating each Series as a partnership for federal tax purposes stands against Recital (c)'s objective that the Trust not be a publicly traded partnership and against the original Section 9.1's statement that the Declaration "creates a trust and not a partnership". Whether the recitals survive the amendment is a live question.

Reaffirming "[a]ll other terms and conditions of the Declaration ... as written" leaves the partnership classification in the amended Section 9.1 sitting alongside Recital (c)'s publicly-traded-partnership objective and Section 4.4's shareholder cap, which the amendment does not address. The blanket reaffirmation does not say how the reaffirmed terms yield to the amendment.
